events.text:
🇮🇷 Democrats could use Vietnam War-style defunding strategy to end Iran crisis
 
“I would stop the funding. The House and the Senate should stop the funding for any further actions in the Iran war. That’s what we did to stop the Vietnam War,” Rep. Ro Khanna told Fox News on the midterms’ eve.
 
👉 Khanna’s Vietnam reference was a nod to an August 1973 maneuver by a Democrat-led Congress, attaching a prohibition on further spending for combat operations in Indochina (North and South Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia) to a must-pass supplemental appropriations bill after President Nixon vetoed a similar motion two months earlier. The measure passed, and the bombing of Cambodia immediately stopped (although financial and military aid to South Vietnam continued until the fall of Saigon in 1975).
 
The California Democrat isn’t alone in pushing the defunding idea, with Just Foreign Policy, a progressive Democrat-allied non-profit, urging the new Congress to “follow its own precedent for how it ended the Vietnam War,” tweeting an updated version of the 1973 measure and suggesting it now include Iran, Yemen, Lebanon and Gaza.
 
‼️ A Times of Israel postmortem of the Democrats’ victory warned [their sweep may have triggered a “countdown”](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77307) toward the Iran war’s conclusion. The article mentioned Vice President Vance’s viral X post naming the Iran war and Republicans’ close ties to Israel as two of the reasons they lost.
But it’s too early to call the Iran war’s end a guarantee in 2027. While incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer have pledged to make ending the crisis a priority, and to use [Congress’s “power of the purse” ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/60938)to do so, they and many of their colleagues have also received substantial AIPAC donations over their careers, and remain staunchly pro-Israel.
Pointing back to the 1973 Vietnam War precedent, it’s worth mentioning that Democrats controlled both Houses of Congress since the war began in 1965, but hawks in their caucus prevented action for years despite calls to do so by lone voices like George McGovern.
